n: In this lecture we study alkaloids containing a xanthine derivative. The outline: caffeine, theobromine and theophylline; their isolation from physical evidence and methods of analysis. Key terms: alkaloids, indole alkaloids, caffeine, theobromine, theophylline, nicotine, anabasine, pachycarpine and spectrophotometric analysis. The topic covers the analysis of substances with weakly basic and neutral properties, and the spectrophotometric method of analysis is also studied.

The chemical nature of purine alkaloids. The alkaloids of the pyrimidine series include the purine alkaloids, that is, caffeine, theophylline and theobromine. They are widely used in medicine and have limited chemical-toxicological significance. By chemical name, caffeine is 1,3,7-trimethylxanthine, theophylline is 1,3-dimethylxanthine, and theobromine is 3,7-dimethylxanthine.

Theophylline and theobromine are isomers of each other. Theophylline, that is, 1,3-dimethylxanthine, is considered an isomer of theobromine, 3,7-dimethylxanthine. Theobromine is found in cocoa and tea leaves. Theophylline is obtained from tea leaves and is synthesised. Theophylline passes from an acidic solution into the organic solvent layer, whereas theobromine does not pass from an alkaline solution.

Sources of purine alkaloids. Purine alkaloids are found in tea, coffee and other plants. Caffeine is also obtained synthetically. For their identification, general precipitating reagents, the murexide reaction and other physicochemical methods are used.

t: Purine derivatives and the isolate scheme
n: The isolate scheme for purine derivatives. In the isolate obtained under acidic conditions, alkaloids with weakly basic properties are examined: caffeine, theobromine, theophylline, papaverine, narcotine and strychnine. In purification by re-extraction, that is, repeated extraction, substances with weakly basic properties, including purine derivatives, are lost. By dry distillation, that is, sublimation, barbiturates, benzoic and salicylic acids, and caffeine can be purified.

Solubility and extraction of caffeine. Caffeine as the base is freely soluble in chloroform, alcohol and water, and sparingly soluble in ether. It is extracted with chloroform mainly under acidic conditions, and partly under alkaline conditions. Solubility ratios: in chloroform 1:5.5, in water 1:46, in ethanol 1:66, in acetone 1:50, in ether 1:530.

t: Extraction of purines: effect of pH
n: The effect of pH is important in the extraction of purines. Caffeine is extracted with chloroform mainly under acidic conditions, and partly under alkaline conditions. Theobromine hardly passes into the organic layer from a caustic alkaline solution, but passes well from an acidic solution. Theophylline passes from an acidic solution into the organic solvent layer.

Pharmacological action of caffeine. Caffeine has a stimulating effect on the central nervous system. It reduces the effect of narcotic and hypnotic drugs and also stimulates the respiratory and other centres. In medicine caffeine is used as the base and as the benzoate and salicylate salts.

Use and significance of caffeine. In fatigue from mental and physical work, taking caffeine is recommended. Caffeine increases the sensitivity of the spinal cord and improves the activity of the heart. It is also used as a preparation that causes copious excretion of urine in the body.

The fate of caffeine in the body. Caffeine is rapidly absorbed and rapidly broken down in the body; only a very small part of it is excreted in the urine. Caffeine has no cumulative effect on the body, that is, it does not accumulate. In terms of toxicity, caffeine is weaker than theophylline, and more strongly toxic than theobromine.

t: Strength of toxic action: theophylline, caffeine, theobromine
n: Let us compare the three substances by strength of toxic action. Caffeine is weaker than theophylline and more strongly toxic than theobromine. That is, theophylline is the strongest, caffeine is in the middle, and theobromine is the weakest. Theobromine stimulates the central nervous system less than caffeine. Purine alkaloids are widely used in medicine and have limited chemical-toxicological significance.

Metabolism of caffeine. Caffeine undergoes metabolism and over 24 hours is excreted from the body in the urine as 1-methylxanthine, 7-methylxanthine, 1,7-dimethylxanthine and 1-methylurea. A very small amount of caffeine is excreted by the kidneys unchanged. From physical evidence it is isolated with acidified water or alcohol under acidic and alkaline conditions.

Caffeine toxicomania, that is, theism. One can become habituated to caffeine. People habituated to caffeine and prone to “theism” brew 25-50 g of dry tea in a small amount of water and drink it at once. Cases of death from caffeine poisoning have been described in the literature.

Physicochemical data of caffeine. International name caffeine, Caffeinum; CAS number 58-08-2; weakly basic in nature. Melting point 234-237 °C. It occurs as white, silky, lustrous needle-like crystals or an odourless, slightly bitter powder. pKa 0.8; half-life 2.3-12 hours.

t: Caffeine: general precipitating reagents and HgCl2
n: The reaction of caffeine with general precipitating reagents and HgCl2. Caffeine gives a precipitate with general precipitating reagents. Under the action of HgCl2 it forms needle-like crystals. For identification, the general precipitating reagents of alkaloids, the murexide reaction and other physicochemical methods are used.

Carrying out the murexide reaction. In the first step the residue under test is treated with an oxidant: bromine or chlorine water, or nitric acid. Then the solution is evaporated on a water bath to dryness. If ammonia solution is added to the residue, a characteristic red colour appears.

The chemistry of the murexide reaction. After oxidation and evaporation, dimethyldialuric acid and dimethylalloxan combine to form tetramethylalloxantin. With ammonia a red colour appears, that is, murexide. Theobromine and theophylline also give this reaction. Therefore the murexide reaction is considered a general reaction for purine derivatives.

Let us summarise the qualitative reactions of caffeine in tabular form. With general precipitating reagents a precipitate forms, and under the action of HgCl2 needle-like crystals. In the murexide reaction the oxidant, evaporation to dryness and ammonia give a red colour; theobromine and theophylline also give it. In TLC the system ether, acetone and 25 % ammonia 40:20:1 is used, and after spraying a violet spot forms. In the UV spectrum the maximum is at 273 nm.

The reaction with Nessler's reagent. If Nessler's reagent is added to an isolate containing caffeine and heated on a water bath, a red-brown precipitate forms. Theobromine gives no precipitate under these conditions. Hence this reaction makes it possible to distinguish caffeine from theobromine.

Identification of caffeine by thin-layer chromatography. System: ether, acetone and 25 % ammonia, 40:20:1. If the plate is sprayed first with 0.1 N iodine solution and then with a mixture of 96 % alcohol and 25 % HCl, 1:1, a violet spot forms. In the qualification analysis another system is also given: methanol and 25 % ammonia 100:1.5; with Dragendorff's reagent a blue spot appears, Rf = 0.52.

t: Caffeine: UV, IR and MS data
n: UV, IR and mass-spectral data of caffeine. A solution of caffeine in ethyl alcohol has a maximum at 273 nm. In a solution in 0.1 M hydrochloric acid the maximum is also observed at 273 nm. In the IR spectrum, in KBr, absorption bands of 658, 1698, 747, 1548, 1242 and 760 cm⁻¹ are given. In the mass spectrum there are peaks at 194, 109, 55, 67, 82, 195, 42 and 110 m/z.

Caffeine: gas chromatography and high-performance liquid chromatography. In GC: glass column 2 m x 2 mm, 3 % SE-30 Chromosorb G-HP, nitrogen 45 ml/min, temperature from 100 to 300 °C; RI 1800. In HPLC: C18 column, 250 x 4.6 mm, 5 µm, 40 °C; mobile phase water, acetonitrile and 2.5 M H2SO4, 50:50:0.1; UV diode-array detector. In HPLC the retention index RI is given as 259.

Quantitative determination of caffeine. The amount is determined by the spectrophotometric, that is, SP, method. Quantification is carried out spectrophotometrically from the UV spectrum, and also by GLC and HPLC methods. A solution of caffeine in ethyl alcohol has a maximum at 273 nm, and the absorbance is measured at this wavelength.

The principle of spectrophotometry. Spectrophotometry is based on measuring monochromatic light in the visible and the adjacent ultraviolet region. The dependence of light absorption on wavelength is called the absorption spectrum of the substance. The absorbance is measured at the wavelength corresponding to the absorption maximum of the test solution.

Conditions of spectrophotometry. In choosing the concentration, the absorbance should lie between 0.2 and 1.0. For one substance in a mixture, the test solution is placed in one cuvette, and all the components of the solution in the other. The solution in the second cuvette is called the reference solution.

The procedure for the spectrophotometric determination of caffeine. For the standard solution, 0.1 g of caffeine is weighed on an analytical balance and placed in a 100 ml volumetric flask. It is first dissolved in a small amount of ethyl alcohol, then made up to the mark with ethyl alcohol. The absorption spectrum is measured in the range 200-400 nm. Caffeine isolated from the object is measured at 273 nm, and the reference solution is ethyl alcohol.

Key figures in caffeine analysis. A solution of caffeine in ethyl alcohol has a maximum at 273 nm; the spectrum is measured in the range 200-400 nm. For the standard solution, 0.1 g of caffeine is dissolved in ethyl alcohol in a 100 ml volumetric flask. The absorbance should lie in the range 0.2-1.0. Theobromine in TLC has Rf = 0.47 ± 0.01.

Theobromine: source and isolation. Theobromine is found in cocoa and tea leaves; it has also been obtained synthetically. On oxidation it breaks down into methylurea and methylalloxan. It hardly passes into the organic layer from a caustic alkaline solution, but passes well from an acidic solution.

Oxidation of theobromine. On oxidation, theobromine breaks down into methylurea and methylalloxan. In the body, as a result of oxidation and N-demethylation, 3-methyl-7-methylxanthine and 7-methyluric acid are formed and excreted in the urine. Theobromine stimulates the central nervous system less than caffeine.

Action and metabolism of theobromine. It stimulates the activity of the heart, dilates the venous vessels of the heart and the bronchial muscles, and increases diuresis. It stimulates the central nervous system less than caffeine; it is used in spasm of the cerebral vessels and chronic coronary disease. In the body, by oxidation and N-demethylation, it forms 3-methyl-7-methylxanthine and 7-methyluric acid and is excreted in the urine.

Qualitative reactions of theobromine. It forms a precipitate with general precipitating reagents. It is freely soluble in CCl4, which distinguishes it from caffeine. With potassium iodobismuthate reagent it forms dark orange needle-like crystals. By TLC, Rf = 0.47±0.01.

Physicochemical data of theobromine. Theobromine is a weak base; CAS 83-67-0; melting point 290-295 °C; pKa 1.1. Solubility: in chloroform 1:6000, in ethanol 1:2220, in water 1:2000; it dissolves in dilute acids and alkalis. From physical evidence it is extracted with acidified water or alcohol at pH 4-7. With Dragendorff's reagent it gives dark orange needle-like crystals.

Source and properties of theophylline. Theophylline is obtained from tea leaves and is synthesised. It passes from an acidic solution into the organic solvent layer. Theophylline is considered an isomer of theobromine.

Use and metabolism of theophylline. In medicine it is used as powder and tablets: euphyllin, theophedrine, antastman. It is used as a diuretic and antiasthmatic, and in ischaemic heart disease. It undergoes metabolism and is excreted in the urine as 1,3-dimethyl-, 3-methyl- and 1-methylurea. Its toxic action is stronger than that of caffeine and theobromine.

Qualitative reactions of theophylline. They are similar to those of caffeine; theophylline also gives the murexide reaction. With diazotised sulphanilic acid it forms a coloured product, which distinguishes it from caffeine and theobromine. In TLC, in the system methanol and 25 % ammonia 100:1.5, Rf = 0.75, blue spot. pKa 8.6; melting point 270-274 °C.

Let us compare the uses of the purine alkaloids in tabular form. Caffeine is used in medicine as the base and as the benzoate and salicylate salts, and stimulates the central nervous system. Theobromine is used as the sodium and salicylate salt, in spasm of the cerebral vessels and chronic coronary disease. Theophylline is used as powder and tablets, under the names euphyllin, theophedrine, antastman; diuretic and antiasthmatic.

How do we distinguish the three purine derivatives? Theobromine is freely soluble in CCl4, which distinguishes it from caffeine. Caffeine gives a precipitate with Nessler's reagent, whereas theobromine does not. Theophylline gives a coloured product with diazotised sulphanilic acid. Thus each substance has its own distinguishing test.

Conclusion on the topic. The purine alkaloids are caffeine, theophylline and theobromine; they are substances with weakly basic and neutral properties and are examined in the acidic isolate. The murexide reaction is general for purine derivatives: oxidation, evaporation, ammonia and a red colour. Caffeine in ethyl alcohol gives a maximum at 273 nm; the absorbance is measured in the range 0.2-1.0. Control questions: how do you distinguish caffeine, theobromine and theophylline? List the stages of the murexide reaction.
